              REPLY BRIEF OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC

           Constellation submits this reply brief1 to address four issues. First, we urge the

Commission to reject PJM’s proposal to delay by three years–until June 2029,2 beyond the second

Trump Administration–the implementation of Interim Network Integration Transmission Service

(“Interim NITS”). There is no good reason for such a delay, which will only harm PJM’s ability

to timely interconnect new data center load while any needed transmission upgrades are being

constructed. Urgency, not delay, is needed. The Commission should therefore establish a separate

track to promptly approve the rates and terms for Interim NITS as modified below and make them

effective no later than October 1, 2026.3 Urgency was a principal motivation for the Commission’s

     I.    The Commission Should Fast Track Interim NITS

           The fastest approach to “release the bottleneck of large load investments across the PJM

footprint”25 and obtain national and economic security is to quickly implement Interim NITS for

new and pending large load applicants. Taking three and half years to implement this transmission

service will not win the AI race, and such delay is inconsistent with the Commission’s

December 18th Order.26 Immediately after the paper hearing briefing concludes, the Commission

should establish a separate track to promptly approve the rates and terms for Interim NITS as

modified below in Section III and make them effective no later than October 1, 2026.

           Five months is a reasonable amount of time to implement this service and advance the

Commission’s goal of speedy interconnection. Indeed, PJM itself has been working on such a

service since at least March 2025 when it suggested its “Option 7” in its Answer to the

February 2025 Show Cause Order.27 Underscoring that there is no barrier to timely

implementation, the Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”) recently committed to making its version of

Interim NITS, Conditional High Impact Large Loads Service (“CHILLS”), available on July 1 of

this year, less than five months after filing its revised tariff proposing the service and less than

three months after SPP’s requested action date by the Commission.28 PJM should be expected to

act with comparable urgency.

             PJM offers no legitimate reason for proposing a three and half year delay. PJM first claims

that Interim NITS “will significantly affect the PJM Load Forecast and expected demand.”29 This

is incorrect. The point of Interim NITS, as the Commission recognized, is that Co-Located Loads

served by Interim NITS are “interruptible loads” and “capacity will not be procured on their behalf

until such time as the Network Upgrades are in place to serve them.”30 PJM has not explained how

Interim NITS will impact its load forecast.

            PJM next claims that the service should be delayed by more than three years because “the

addition of the three new transmission services will require significant changes to PJM’s core

Markets and Operations systems”31 as they do not currently “automate Curtailment of Non-Firm

Contract Demand Transmission Service (or Interim NITS) before Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service.”32 PJM implies implementing these changes could be delayed by “vendor

availability, the speed with which the system changes can be designed, and the interaction of these

requested changes with other competing priorities.”33 Possible logistical challenges will not risk

delay if the Commission separates and implements Interim NITS on a fast track. Like SPP, PJM

will only need to automate curtailment of Interim NITS before NITS just as it does for external

Non-Firm Point to Point Transmission Service. Before entering Emergency Procedures, “PJM

PJM also interrupts non-firm service for economic reasons to accommodate “a request for Firm

            Last, PJM argues the more-than-three-year delay is necessary because it “does not expect

that Eligible Customers and associated generation will be online and taking service under any of

the proposed transmission services before June 1, 2029.”36 This rationale ignores—and effectively

precludes—load co-locating with existing generation from selecting Interim NITS. Existing

generators can serve Co-Located Loads after completing required Network Upgrades, and,

consistent with the December 18th Order, PJM should be trying to promote speedy connection,

including through co-location arrangements with existing generation, rather than to stymie such

arrangements. Speed to service will not be achieved if discrimination is allowed against all the

megawatts already available and ready to reliably serve.

  II.        PJM Proposes to Restrict Contract Demand Services in Conflict with the December 18th

 2   Q19. WHAT IS THE APPROPRIATE BASIS FOR DETERMINING A GRID

 3          RELIANCE CHARGE (“GRC”)?

 4   A19.   Customers subject to the GRC are, by definition, not drawing power from the PJM

 5          network in order to serve their load. If they were drawing power from the system

 6          to serve their load, they would be required to purchase Firm or Non-Firm Contract

 7          Demand Service. In this sense, co-located load customers receive ancillary services

 8          from the existence of the wires that synchronize them to the rest of the PJM system.

 9                 However, PJM’s wires are sized and built to serve PJM’s actual peak

10          demand. That creates a cost causation distinction. The incremental costs of sizing

11          the PJM system to serve actual peak demand should reasonably be borne by

12          customers who cause this demand, while customers benefitting from the existence

13          of the wires should be responsible for their share of costs that would be necessary

14          to construct the wires without sizing them to meet peak demand. Within the context

15          of electricity system ratemaking, there is a well-established methodology designed

16          to calculate precisely the costs of constructing wires to connect all customers, i.e.,

17          customer-driven costs. It is called the “minimum system” method.


18   Q20. WHAT IS A “MINIMUM SYSTEM”?

19   A20.   A “minimum system” is a theoretical electricity system designed only to connect

20          each customer and deliver a de minimis amount of power. An analyst can calculate

21          the cost of such a system by determining the minimum size of all electricity system




                                               14
  1          components (e.g., poles, conductors, transformers, etc.) that could be used by the

 2          utility to recreate its system and connect each customer to the grid.


 3   Q21. IS     THE     MINIMUM         SYSTEM       METHOD         RELATED        TO    COST

 4          CAUSATION PRINCIPLES?

 5   A21.   Yes. The minimum system method is specifically designed to identify the portion

 6          of system costs that are customer-driven rather than demand- or energy-driven. It

 7          answers the question of what it would cost to construct a system to connect all

 8          customers before the system is upsized to serve actual peak demand or energy

 9          usage. That is precisely relevant to the question at hand. Co-located load subject to

10          the GRC benefits from the existence of wires but, by definition, does not impose

11          any demand on the PJM system. The minimum system framework therefore

12          provides the appropriate cost causation-aligned methodology for calculating the

13          GRC.


14   Q22. DOES THE MINIMUM SYSTEM FRAMEWORK HAVE PRECEDENT IN

15          ELECTRICITY SECTOR RATEMAKING?

16   A22.   Yes. The minimum system framework has substantial precedent in electricity-

17          sector ratemaking, particularly in distribution cost allocation and rate design. It is

18          widely used to identify the portion of system costs that are customer-driven; that is,

19          costs incurred because the customer is connected to the system. NARUC recognizes

20          this framework, referring to it as the “minimum-size method,” as one of the “[t]wo

21          methods … used to determine the … customer components of distribution




                                               15

 2           to serve higher levels of demand that should be appropriately allocated based on

 3           how much demand each customer is drawing from the network.

 4                    Many utilities within PJM use minimum system studies in distribution cost

 5           allocation, including at least two Indicated PJM Transmission Owners: PPL

 6           Electric Utilities Corporation22 and FirstEnergy Service Company.23


 7   Q23. IS THE MINIMUM SYSTEM METHOD TYPICALLY USED IN THE

 8           CONTEXT OF THE TRANSMISSION SYSTEM AND WHY?

 9   A23.    The minimum system method is generally not used in the context of transmission

10           system cost allocation and rate design. Transmission system components are

11           generally much larger and more costly relative to a minimum system. This

12           inherently shrinks the quantity of costs that could be customer-classified and makes

13           the need to perform this step less important. Additionally, transmission

14           customers—whether large individual loads or aggregations of smaller loads—have

15           traditionally imposed a meaningful level of demand on the system, meaning there

16           has not been a significant need to allocate a portion of transmission system costs to

17           customers that are not actually drawing power from the grid. Against this backdrop,

18           utilities typically allocate transmission costs largely on the basis of demand. In

19           effect, this classifies 0% of transmission costs to the “customer” cost driver.

10   Q32. WHAT ARE THE IMPACTS OF A GRC THAT IS TOO HIGH?

11   A32.    Customers that pay the GRC by definition do not impose any incremental cost on

12           the transmission system. Thus, all GRC charges that the Transmission Owners

13           collect are used to directly reduce the NITS rate for all other customers.28 In this

14           regard, it may seem that a higher GRC rate would yield higher GRC revenues and

15           thus higher reductions to the NITS rate for all other customers. However, basic

16           economics tells us that this is not necessarily the case. As Art Laffer artfully

17           demonstrated, higher tax rates can actually yield lower tax revenues to the extent

18           that they discourage work and investment.29

19                    In the case of the GRC, inappropriately increasing the rate to too high of a

20           level could have the effect of reducing absolute GRC revenues for two reasons.

21           First, it could discourage the development of co-located load in the PJM region.
